## What I do

I am a spatial data scientist and public health professional working at the intersection of GIS, mosquito control, drones, and field operations. I build systems that turn data from traps, laboratories, aircraft, and field crews into information people can use to make better decisions.

At Collier Mosquito Control District, I lead technical development across GIS, spatial analytics, and unmanned aircraft systems. Much of my work involves connecting pieces that are often treated separately, including surveillance data, environmental conditions, treatment records, remote sensing, and the practical realities of field operations.

I enjoy working on problems where analysis has a visible operational outcome. That might mean improving how an aerial treatment is calibrated, helping a field team prioritize an area, or making complex surveillance information easier to understand and act on. The tools vary from project to project, but the goal is consistent: produce reliable information that supports effective and defensible public health decisions.

## How I got here

I did not begin my career expecting to work in spatial data science. I studied philosophy at the University of North Texas and entered mosquito control through hands-on field surveillance. Setting traps, identifying mosquitoes, maintaining equipment, and coordinating field activities gave me an appreciation for how much public health decisions depend on the quality and context of the underlying data.

My interest in GIS grew from wanting to solve practical problems that were difficult to understand from tables alone. One of my earliest GIS projects brought together a county storm sewer dataset and the locations of *Culex quinquefasciatus* mosquito pools that had tested positive for West Nile virus. By examining where positive-pool hotspots aligned with the storm sewer network, I used the existing infrastructure data to identify potential underground breeding sites and help plan a more focused surveillance and response strategy.

That project showed me how geographic information could connect surveillance results to features in the environment and turn an observed pattern into a practical course of action. It led me further into GIS, programming, data visualization, and spatial analysis. Over time, my work expanded from organizing individual surveillance routes to developing organization-wide data systems, operational dashboards, aerial application analyses, and drone-based remote-sensing workflows.

I later completed a graduate certificate in geographic information systems and a master's degree in spatial data science at Penn State. My education strengthened the analytical foundation behind work that has always remained grounded in field operations and applied public health.

## Research and professional interests

I am especially interested in spatial decision-support systems, drone-based remote sensing, and better ways to evaluate and calibrate aerial applications. My recent work includes characterizing granular larvicide swaths, modeling application overlap, using drone-based LiDAR to study mosquito habitat, and developing reproducible tools that make rigorous analysis more accessible to operational teams.

I am also interested in the less visible work that makes technical systems useful over time: thoughtful data structures, clear documentation, quality control, training, and workflows that other people can understand and maintain. A successful tool should do more than produce an answer once. It should help an organization make better decisions consistently.

## A little more about me

I am a generalist at heart. I enjoy learning how systems work, finding connections across disciplines, and making things that are useful. Depending on the problem, that might involve writing code, working through a map, designing a custom part, testing a piece of field equipment, or translating a technical result for a broader audience.

What continues to draw me to this work is the combination of curiosity, practicality, and public service. Spatial data science gives me a way to explore complicated questions while staying connected to the people, places, and day-to-day decisions the analysis is meant to support.
